7.1: The Hebrew separately says the men came, brought the ark up, and brought it into the house. BSB combines the latter movements and leaves the upward direction implicit.
7.2: The Hebrew describes the passing of time with “the days multiplied”; BSB says “a long time passed.”
7.3: The Hebrew twice uses singular “your heart”; BSB uses plural “your hearts.”
7.6: The Hebrew introduces their words with the general “they said”; BSB specifies “they confessed.”
7.7: The Hebrew explicitly calls the advancing rulers “the rulers of the Philistines”; BSB uses “their rulers.”
7.8: The Hebrew explicitly repeats “the sons of Israel” as the speakers; BSB carries them forward as the unnamed subject of “said.”
7.9: The Hebrew repeats Samuel’s name before his crying out; BSB uses “He.”
7.10: The Hebrew says the Philistines “were defeated” before Israel; BSB says “they fled.” It describes the thunder with “a great voice,” rendered “loudly” in BSB.
7.14: The Hebrew describes the cities as returning, where BSB uses passive “were restored.” It explicitly says the Philistines had taken them from Israel and uses collective singular “the Amorite” rather than plural “the Amorites.”
7.17: The Hebrew repeats “there” for the home, the judging, and the altar-building. BSB states it for the first two and leaves it implicit for the altar.

8.3: The Hebrew uses separate finite verbs for taking a bribe and perverting judgment; BSB makes these actions participles. It has singular “a bribe,” rendered plural “bribes” in BSB.
8.6: The Hebrew repeats Samuel’s name as the subject of praying; BSB uses “he.”
8.7: The Hebrew describes rejection of the LORD’s “reigning over them”; BSB expresses this as rejecting Him “as their king.”
8.8: The Hebrew says they do this to “you also”; BSB leaves the “also” implicit.
8.9: The Hebrew commands listening to “their voice”; BSB says “listen to them.”
8.11: The Hebrew uses singular “his chariot” in both occurrences; BSB uses plural “his chariots.” It names his horsemen, where BSB has “horses.”
8.12: The Hebrew pairs plowing with his plowing-land and reaping with his harvest, repeating the respective roots. It names the equipment of his chariot, where BSB turns this into the action “to equip his chariots.”
8.15: The Hebrew names their “seed” and “vineyards”; BSB renders these as “grain and grape harvest.”
8.16: The Hebrew names their best “young men”; BSB has “best cattle.”
8.18: The Hebrew says they will “cry out” because of their king; BSB specifies that they will “beg for relief.”
8.19: The Hebrew mentions “the voice of Samuel” and says a king “shall be over us”; BSB omits the voice image and renders the demand as “We must have a king.”
8.20: The Hebrew calls the king “our king”; BSB uses “a king.”
8.21: The Hebrew says Samuel spoke the words “in the ears of the LORD”; BSB renders the bodily image as “in the hearing of the LORD.”
8.22: The Hebrew commands them to “go, each to his city”; BSB adds an explicit return in “go back.”

9.1: The Hebrew ends the genealogy with “son of a Benjamite man”; BSB compresses this to “of Benjamin.”
9.2: The Hebrew describes his height as “from his shoulder and upward” above the people; BSB renders this as “a head taller.”
9.3: The Hebrew specifically names female donkeys and has no separate introductory “One day.” It also includes a request particle and a separate command to rise, left implicit in BSB.
9.4: The Hebrew leaves Saul unnamed and repeats the verb for passing through four times. BSB supplies Saul and the servant and varies the wording of the journey.
9.6: The Hebrew leaves the speaker unnamed, where BSB supplies “the servant.” It refers to “our way on which we have gone”; BSB instead says “which way to go.”
9.7: The Hebrew explicitly says Saul spoke “to his servant.” It describes the containers as “our vessels”; BSB uses “our packs.”
9.8: The Hebrew explicitly names Saul as the recipient of the answer; BSB uses “him.”
9.10: The Hebrew says “your word is good”; BSB retains only “Good.”
9.12: The Hebrew repeats “today” when explaining both his arrival and the sacrifice; BSB states it only for his arrival.
9.13: The Hebrew’s final assurance of finding him again includes an expression referring to today; BSB leaves this time reference implicit.
9.14: The Hebrew leaves the travelers unnamed; BSB identifies them as Saul and his servant.
9.15: The Hebrew uses the image of the LORD uncovering Samuel’s ear; BSB renders it as revealing something to Samuel.
9.16: The Hebrew repeats “My people” as those he will save; BSB substitutes “them.”
9.19: The Hebrew joins sending Saul away and telling him what is in his heart as separate statements. BSB makes the sending a “when” clause introducing the telling.
9.20: The Hebrew says not to “set your heart” on the donkeys; BSB renders this bodily expression as “do not worry about them.”
9.21: The Hebrew describes Benjamin as among the small tribes, using a plural expression; BSB calls it “the smallest tribe.”
9.22: The Hebrew says Samuel gave them a place “at the head” of the invited guests; BSB renders this as “the place of honor.”
9.24: The Hebrew leaves the speaker of the instructions unnamed; BSB explicitly identifies him as Samuel.
9.25: The Hebrew leaves the speaker unnamed and says simply “on the roof”; BSB supplies Samuel and expands the location to “the roof of his house.”
9.26: The Hebrew places the call at the rising of dawn; BSB says “just before dawn.” The command literally says “rise,” rendered “Get ready” in BSB.
9.27: The Hebrew reports the servant’s departure before the command for Saul to stand; BSB moves it to the end. It says Samuel will “cause you to hear” God’s word, rendered “reveal to you” in BSB.

10.1: The Hebrew leaves the recipient of the oil unnamed; BSB supplies Saul in “Saul’s head.”
10.2: The Hebrew explicitly refers to abandoning “the matters of the donkeys”; BSB renders this as stopping worrying about them.
10.4: The Hebrew says they will ask about his “peace” or welfare; BSB says they will “greet” him. It uses singular “their hand,” rendered plural “their hands” in BSB.
10.5: The Hebrew names the harp, tambourine, flute, and lyre in the singular; BSB makes all four plural. It also uses a plural expression for the Philistine stations, where BSB has “an outpost.”
10.7: The Hebrew commands doing what “your hand finds”; BSB replaces this bodily image with “as the occasion demands.”
10.8: The Hebrew explicitly describes going down to Gilgal and Samuel coming down to him; BSB leaves both downward directions implicit.
10.9: The Hebrew leaves Saul unnamed and describes his turning with “his shoulder.” God changes for him “another heart”; BSB supplies Saul’s name and says God “changed Saul’s heart.”
10.10: The Hebrew leaves the arriving travelers unnamed; BSB identifies them as Saul and his servant.
10.11: The Hebrew describes prior knowledge with “yesterday, the day before yesterday”; BSB uses “formerly.”
10.13: The Hebrew leaves Saul unnamed and says he came to the high place; BSB names Saul and supplies the upward direction in “went up.”
10.14: The Hebrew leaves the respondent unnamed; BSB identifies him as Saul.
10.15: The Hebrew includes a request particle in “tell me, please”; BSB leaves the politeness particle implicit.
10.16: The Hebrew leaves the subject of not telling unnamed and uses “him” as the recipient; BSB explicitly names Saul and his uncle in that clause.
10.18: The Hebrew uses singular “hand” twice and names Egypt collectively; BSB uses plural “hands” and “the Egyptians.”
10.19: The Hebrew calls the family groups “your thousands”; BSB renders this as “clans.”
10.21: The Hebrew says passively that he “was not found”; BSB changes this to active “they could not find him.”
10.23: The Hebrew leaves the fetched man unnamed and describes his height from his shoulder upward. BSB supplies Saul and renders the height as “a head taller.”
10.27: The Hebrew calls the dissenters “sons of worthlessness” and says he was “like one keeping silent.” BSB uses “worthless men” and says Saul “remained silent about it.” The Hebrew has singular “a gift,” rendered plural “gifts” in BSB.

11.1: The Hebrew says to “cut a covenant” and explicitly names Nahash as the recipient of the men’s words. BSB uses “Make a treaty” and refers to him as “him.”
11.3: The Hebrew says “we will come out to you”; BSB makes the submission explicit with “we will surrender to you.”
11.4: The Hebrew says they spoke “in the ears of the people,” then that the people lifted their voice and wept. BSB uses “in the hearing” and “wept aloud.”
11.5: The Hebrew says Saul was coming from the field behind the cattle; BSB explicitly makes this a return and supplies the possessive “his oxen.”
11.6: The Hebrew describes his anger through the image of his nose burning; BSB renders this as burning “with great anger.”
11.7: The Hebrew says the pieces were sent “by the hand of the messengers”; BSB leaves the hand image implicit.
11.8: The Hebrew leaves the one numbering unnamed and uses collective singular “man of Judah.” BSB supplies Saul and uses plural “men of Judah.”
11.10: The Hebrew says “we will come out to you” and describes what is “good in your eyes.” BSB supplies Nahash as the addressee and leaves both “to you” and the eyes image implicit.
11.11: The Hebrew calls the divisions “three heads” and names Ammon collectively; BSB has “three divisions” and “the Ammonites.” It says until the heat of the day, without an explicit superlative corresponding to “hottest.”
11.12: The Hebrew quotes the dissenting words as “Shall Saul reign over us?” without an explicit negative. BSB adds “not” in “Saul should not reign over us.”
11.13: The Hebrew introduces Saul’s words with the general “said”; BSB specifies that he “ordered.”
11.15: The Hebrew twice names Gilgal and twice uses “there” for the sacrificing and rejoicing; BSB names Gilgal once and uses “There” once. It describes making Saul king, where BSB says they “confirmed” him as king.

16.1: The Hebrew says the LORD has “seen” a king for Himself among Jesse’s sons; BSB renders this as “selected.”
16.2: The Hebrew commands taking the heifer “in your hand”; BSB renders this as taking it “with you.”
16.6: The Hebrew leaves the one seeing Eliab unnamed; BSB supplies Samuel.
16.7: The Hebrew says a person sees “to the eyes,” retaining an eyes image; BSB renders this as seeing “the outward appearance.”
16.8: The Hebrew says Jesse made Abinadab pass before Samuel; BSB renders this movement as presenting him to Samuel.
16.9: The Hebrew says Jesse made Shammah pass and leaves the following speaker unnamed. BSB uses “presented” and explicitly identifies Samuel as the speaker.
16.10: The Hebrew explicitly names Jesse as the recipient of Samuel’s reply; BSB uses “him.”
16.11: The Hebrew has no separate verb corresponding to eating in “we will not sit down to eat.” BSB also identifies the respondent as Jesse, where the Hebrew leaves him unnamed.
16.12: The Hebrew says “he sent and brought him”; BSB supplies Jesse and “his youngest son.”
16.14: The Hebrew calls the troubling spirit “evil”; BSB uses “a spirit of distress.” It has no separate verb meaning “began.”
16.15: The Hebrew calls it an “evil spirit of God”; BSB uses “a spirit of distress from God.”
16.16: The Hebrew calls the spirit “evil” and explicitly says the musician will play “with his hand”; BSB uses “of distress” and leaves the hand implicit.
16.17: The Hebrew introduces the words with “said” and includes a request particle; BSB specifies that Saul “commanded.”
16.18: The Hebrew says Jesse’s son knows how to play, without naming the instrument here; BSB supplies “the harp.”
16.20: The Hebrew says the gifts were sent “by the hand of David”; BSB renders this as “with his son David.”
16.21: The Hebrew says David stood before Saul and that Saul loved him greatly; BSB uses “entered his service” and “admired him greatly.”
16.22: The Hebrew asks that David “stand before me” and says he has “found favor in my eyes.” BSB renders these as remaining in Saul’s service and “I am pleased with him.”
16.23: The Hebrew separately describes relief for Saul and his becoming well, and explicitly mentions David playing with his hand. BSB combines the result as becoming well and leaves the hand implicit; it calls the evil spirit a “spirit of distress.”

17.1: The Hebrew uses two gathering verbs, first for their forces and then for assembling at Socoh; BSB combines these into one gathering statement.
17.4: The Hebrew uses plural “camps of the Philistines”; BSB uses singular “the Philistine camp.”
17.5: The Hebrew describes the armor as a coat of “scales”; BSB uses “coat of mail.”
17.7: The Hebrew calls the spear’s shaft its “wood” and its point its “flame.” It uses plural “weavers” in the beam comparison, where BSB has singular “a weaver.”
17.8: The Hebrew leaves the speaker unnamed; BSB supplies Goliath. He calls himself “the Philistine,” whereas BSB has “a Philistine.”
17.9: The Hebrew twice uses a verb meaning “strike”; BSB renders both occurrences as “kill.”
17.10: The Hebrew says “Give me a man, and let us fight together”; BSB compresses this to “Give me a man to fight.”
17.12: The Hebrew calls Jesse “the man” in the final clause; BSB repeats his name.
17.13: The Hebrew repeats the verb for going in describing the older sons and explicitly introduces the names of the three sons. BSB combines this into one following statement and a list.
17.17: The Hebrew has no separate introductory “One day” and includes a request particle in the instruction to take the food; BSB adds the time expression and leaves the request particle implicit.
17.18: The Hebrew calls the officer “commander of the thousand”; BSB renders the number as the more general “their unit.”
17.21: The Hebrew repeats “battle line” in “battle line against battle line”; BSB combines this into “in formation against each other.”
17.22: The Hebrew says David left his equipment “at the hand of the keeper of the equipment”; BSB renders this as leaving supplies “in the care of the quartermaster.”
17.23: The Hebrew says he “spoke according to these words”; BSB describes him as shouting “his usual words.”
17.24: The Hebrew calls the one seen “the man”; BSB supplies Goliath.
17.25: The Hebrew says the king will make the father’s house “free in Israel”; BSB specifies that the freedom is “from taxation.”
17.29: The Hebrew’s final question uses the general noun for a word or matter; BSB specifies “a question.”
17.30: The Hebrew says he spoke the same words to another person; BSB specifies that he “asked about the offer.”
17.31: The Hebrew actively says unnamed people reported the words, then that Saul took David. BSB uses passive “reported to Saul” and says Saul “called for him.”
17.32: The Hebrew uses “him” in the first clause and names “this Philistine” in the second; BSB names the Philistine first and then uses “him.”
17.34: The Hebrew explicitly names Saul as the recipient and joins the lion and bear with “and”; BSB leaves the addressee implicit and uses “or.”
17.35: The Hebrew says David seized the animal by its “beard”; BSB renders this as “fur.”
17.36: The Hebrew has singular “the lion” and “the bear” and uses a verb for striking; BSB has plural “lions and bears” and uses “killed.”
17.37: The Hebrew repeats “hand” for the lion and the bear; BSB combines these as their “claws.”
17.38: The Hebrew calls the clothing “his garments” in the plural; BSB uses singular “his own tunic.”
17.39: The Hebrew twice uses the verb for testing or trying in explaining his difficulty walking; BSB renders both as being “not accustomed.” The garments are plural, where BSB has singular “tunic.”
17.40: The Hebrew leaves David unnamed and refers to the shepherds collectively in the plural. BSB supplies David and uses singular “his shepherd’s bag.”
17.43: The Hebrew names the speaker “the Philistine” in the first clause; BSB uses “he.”
17.44: The Hebrew again names the speaker “the Philistine”; BSB uses “he.”
17.46: The Hebrew describes a carcass of the Philistine camp collectively in the singular; BSB uses plural “carcasses of the Philistines.” The final statement says there is a God “for Israel,” where BSB has “in Israel.”
17.47: The Hebrew uses singular “our hand”; BSB uses plural “our hands.”
17.48: The Hebrew repeats David and the Philistine as the advancing parties; BSB replaces both with pronouns in parts of the verse.
17.49: The Hebrew explicitly says David sent his hand into the container; BSB compresses this to reaching into his bag.
17.50: The Hebrew repeats David’s name in the final statement about the sword; BSB refers to “his hand.”
17.52: The Hebrew says the slain Philistines “fell” along the road; BSB describes their bodies as being “strewn” there.
17.54: The Hebrew refers to “his equipment” without repeating the Philistine’s name; BSB supplies “Goliath’s weapons.”
17.55: The Hebrew’s oath says “as your soul lives”; BSB leaves the soul image implicit in “As surely as you live.”
17.56: The Hebrew commands the hearer to “ask” whose son he is; BSB uses “Find out.”
17.57: The Hebrew explicitly repeats “the head of the Philistine”; BSB uses “his head” and supplies “still.”

18.1: The Hebrew leaves David unnamed in the opening clause and says Jonathan’s soul was bound to David’s soul. BSB supplies David and makes the two souls a combined subject; it renders the final “his soul” as “himself.”
18.2: The Hebrew leaves David unnamed and says Saul took him “on that day”; BSB supplies David and says “from that day.”
18.3: The Hebrew says Jonathan and David “cut a covenant”; BSB says Jonathan “made a covenant with David.” The final love expression literally refers to “his soul.”
18.4: The Hebrew has plural “his garments”; BSB uses singular “his tunic.”
18.5: The Hebrew twice uses “in the eyes” for the people and Saul’s servants; BSB combines both under one “in the sight.” It renders the servants as “officers.”
18.6: The Hebrew leaves the arriving group unnamed; BSB supplies “the troops” and “home.” The Hebrew names joy, where BSB makes this “joyful songs.”
18.7: The Hebrew says the women answered and said; BSB combines these into “sang out.”
18.8: The Hebrew says this “word” was evil in Saul’s eyes; BSB specifies “this song” and renders the eyes image as resentment.
18.10: The Hebrew calls it an “evil spirit of God”; BSB has “a spirit of distress sent from God.” It names David’s playing hand without naming the instrument, where BSB supplies the harp.
18.11: The Hebrew explicitly says Saul hurled “the spear” and introduces his words with “said”; BSB uses “he hurled it” and “thinking.” It repeats David as the one evading him.
18.12: The Hebrew says the LORD was “with him”; BSB supplies David’s name.
18.13: The Hebrew says he “went out and came in before the people”; BSB expands this to leading troops out to battle and back.
18.14: The Hebrew names David and joins his success and the LORD’s presence with “and”; BSB uses “he” and makes the LORD’s presence an explicit “because” clause.
18.15: The Hebrew says Saul saw that “he” was successful; BSB supplies David.
18.16: The Hebrew says David was “going out and coming in before them”; BSB expands this to leading them out to battle and back.
18.17: The Hebrew introduces Saul’s private words with “said” and says his hand should not be against David; BSB has “was thinking” and adds the action of raising the hand.
18.20: The Hebrew actively says unnamed people told Saul, and that the matter was right in his eyes. BSB uses passive “was reported” and renders the eyes image as “it pleased him.”
18.21: The Hebrew says “I will give her to him”; BSB supplies David. It introduces the statement with “said,” rendered “thought” in BSB.
18.23: The Hebrew says Saul’s servants spoke “in David’s ears”; BSB simply says they relayed the words to him.
18.24: The Hebrew explicitly calls them “Saul’s servants” and quotes their report. BSB leaves the possessive implicit and makes the report indirect.
18.25: The Hebrew says Saul planned to cause David to “fall into the hand of the Philistines”; BSB makes the death explicit and uses plural “hands.”
18.26: The Hebrew says “the days were not full”; BSB specifies “Before the wedding day arrived.” It also renders the matter being right in David’s eyes as his being pleased.
18.27: The Hebrew repeats David’s name for bringing the foreskins; BSB uses “He.” In the final giving of Michal, the Hebrew uses “him,” where BSB supplies David.
18.28: The Hebrew separately says Saul saw and knew; BSB combines these as “realized.” It calls Michal “Saul’s daughter” and refers to the one loved as “him”; BSB has “his daughter” and names David.
18.29: The Hebrew names Saul at the start of his increasing fear; BSB uses “he.”
18.30: The Hebrew first says the commanders went out, then speaks of each time they went out; BSB combines these into one time clause and supplies “for battle.”

19.1: The Hebrew repeats Jonathan’s identity as “son of Saul” in the second clause; BSB leaves this description implicit.
19.3: The Hebrew says Jonathan will speak about David to his father; BSB makes this specifically asking about him. Jonathan then says he will see what happens, where BSB has an “if I find out anything” clause.
19.5: The Hebrew says David placed his “soul in his palm,” both singular; BSB uses “life in his hands.”
19.6: The Hebrew repeats Saul’s name before his oath and leaves the person not to be killed unnamed; BSB omits the repeated Saul and supplies David.
19.7: The Hebrew names Jonathan three times and says David was before Saul “as yesterday, the day before yesterday.” BSB names Jonathan twice and renders the time expression as serving him “as he had before.”
19.9: The Hebrew calls the spirit “evil” and explicitly names David’s playing hand without naming the instrument. BSB uses “a spirit of distress” and supplies “the harp.”
19.10: The Hebrew actively describes Saul driving the spear into the wall; BSB makes the spear itself the subject of striking the wall.
19.11: The Hebrew describes the threatened fate with passive “you are being put to death”; BSB states the result as “you will be dead.”
19.12: The Hebrew uses three verbs for going, fleeing, and escaping; BSB combines the first two as “ran away.”
19.13: The Hebrew uses the plural form “teraphim”; BSB has singular “a household idol.”
19.14: The Hebrew leaves the woman speaking unnamed; BSB identifies her as Michal.
19.15: The Hebrew has no separate word for “back” in Saul’s sending of the messengers.
19.16: The Hebrew again uses plural “teraphim”; BSB has singular “the idol.”
19.17: The Hebrew gives David’s threat as “Why should I kill you?”; BSB turns this into “or I will kill you!”
19.20: The Hebrew explicitly names Saul as the sender and David as the one to be seized; BSB uses pronouns. Samuel is described as standing over the prophets, rendered “leading them” in BSB.
19.21: The Hebrew actively says unnamed people told Saul; BSB uses passive “this was reported to Saul.”
19.22: The Hebrew leaves both the traveler and the answering speaker unnamed; BSB identifies the traveler as Saul and makes the reply passive “he was told.”
19.23: The Hebrew uses pronouns for Saul twice; BSB names him twice.
19.24: The Hebrew says he fell naked, with a time expression covering day and night; BSB supplies a separate “lay” verb and names Saul where the Hebrew uses a pronoun.

20.1: The Hebrew asks “What is my sin before your father?” and says he seeks David’s soul. BSB makes the question verbal, “How have I sinned,” and renders seeking the soul as wanting to take his life.
20.2: The Hebrew leaves the speaker unnamed and describes disclosure as uncovering his ear. BSB supplies Jonathan and uses “telling me.”
20.3: The Hebrew’s oath explicitly invokes “your soul” living; BSB renders this as “you yourself” living.
20.4: The Hebrew asks what David’s “soul says”; BSB renders this as “Whatever you desire.”
20.5: The Hebrew explicitly names Jonathan as recipient and repeats the sitting root in the expected meal. BSB uses “him” and renders the expectation as “I am supposed to dine.”
20.7: The Hebrew says there is “peace for your servant”; BSB says “your servant is safe.” It describes evil as determined by the father, rendered “he has evil intentions.”
20.8: The Hebrew repeats “your servant” and calls the agreement “a covenant of the LORD”; BSB uses “me” and “a covenant with you before the LORD.”
20.11: The Hebrew explicitly names Jonathan speaking to David; BSB uses “he replied.”
20.12: The Hebrew names David as the one toward whom the father may be favorable; BSB uses “you.” Its disclosure image is uncovering the ear, rendered “tell you.”
20.13: The Hebrew’s oath names Jonathan, where BSB uses “me.” It says to uncover David’s ear and send him in peace; BSB uses telling him and sending him “in safety.”
20.16: The Hebrew’s accountability expression is seeking “from the hand of David’s enemies”; BSB leaves the hand image implicit in holding them accountable.
20.17: The Hebrew leaves the loving subjects and objects as pronouns and explicitly names love of his soul. BSB supplies Jonathan and David and renders the soul as “himself.”
20.18: The Hebrew pairs two forms of the same missing or attending root; BSB uses “be missed” and “is empty.”
20.19: The Hebrew calls the earlier occasion “the day of the deed”; BSB specifies “the day this trouble began.”
20.21: The Hebrew says “there is no matter” against David; BSB specifies “there is no danger.”
20.23: The Hebrew says the LORD is between them forever; BSB supplies “a witness.”
20.24: The Hebrew explicitly says the king sat to the bread to eat; BSB leaves the bread implicit.
20.25: The Hebrew says Jonathan rose and Abner sat beside Saul; BSB instead describes the king sitting opposite Jonathan and beside Abner.
20.26: The Hebrew leaves David unnamed and has no separate term corresponding to “ceremonially”; BSB supplies both.
20.27: The Hebrew again calls the meal “the bread”; BSB uses “the meal.”
20.28: The Hebrew explicitly names Saul as the recipient of the answer; BSB leaves him implicit.
20.30: The Hebrew’s final shame expression explicitly refers to “the nakedness of your mother”; BSB instead says “the mother who bore you.”
20.31: The Hebrew calls David “a son of death”; BSB renders this image as “he must surely die.”
20.32: The Hebrew explicitly says Jonathan answered his father Saul; BSB leaves the addressee implicit.
20.33: The Hebrew leaves Jonathan unnamed as the spear’s target and uses a verb for striking him; BSB supplies Jonathan and says “to kill him.”
20.34: The Hebrew calls what he did not eat “bread”; BSB uses “any food.” It gives his grief over David and his father’s shaming as separate clauses, which BSB combines.
20.36: The Hebrew includes a request particle in the order to find the arrows; BSB leaves it implicit and supplies Jonathan as the shooter where the Hebrew uses “he.”
20.37: The Hebrew says the boy reached the arrow’s place which Jonathan had shot; BSB supplies the arrow’s having fallen there.
20.38: The Hebrew calls him “Jonathan’s boy” and names plural “arrows”; BSB uses “the boy” and singular “the arrow.”
20.40: The Hebrew commands taking the equipment into the city, without a separate “back”; BSB supplies “back.”
20.41: The Hebrew says David rose from beside the south, without explicitly naming the stone here. BSB supplies “of the stone” and names Jonathan as David’s partner where the Hebrew uses reciprocal expressions.
20.42: The Hebrew’s oath says the LORD is between them; BSB supplies “a witness.” It uses the seed image for descendants, leaves David unnamed at his departure, and says Jonathan came into the city rather than explicitly went back.

3.1: The Hebrew has singular “vision” and describes it as not spreading widely; BSB uses plural “visions” and calls them “scarce.”
3.2: The Hebrew says Eli’s eyes had begun to grow dim and calls his location “his place.” BSB says his eyesight “had grown so dim” and places him “in his room.”
3.5: The Hebrew leaves the replying speaker unnamed; BSB supplies Eli.
3.6: The Hebrew again leaves the replying speaker unnamed; BSB supplies Eli.
3.7: The Hebrew joins the two statements with “and”; BSB makes the lack of revelation an explicit “because” clause.
3.9: The Hebrew explicitly names Eli as speaker; BSB uses “he.”
3.11: The Hebrew explicitly names the hearer’s “two ears”; BSB leaves the number implicit.
3.13: The Hebrew uses a pronominal expression “for themselves” in the clause about the sons’ cursing; BSB explicitly names God as the object of blasphemy.
3.15: The Hebrew repeats Samuel’s name in describing his fear; BSB uses “He.”
3.16: The Hebrew explicitly names Samuel as the one called and leaves the respondent unnamed; BSB uses “him” for the one called and supplies Samuel as respondent.
3.17: The Hebrew leaves Eli unnamed and has a request particle in the prohibition. Its oath literally says “thus may God do to you, and thus may He add”; BSB makes the punishment and severity explicit.
3.18: The Hebrew leaves the replying speaker unnamed; BSB supplies Eli.
3.19: The Hebrew refers to “his words” without repeating Samuel’s name; BSB explicitly says “Samuel’s words.”
3.21: The Hebrew repeats the LORD’s name three times and Shiloh twice; BSB names each once and uses pronouns for the other occurrences.

4.3: The Hebrew calls those arriving “the people”; BSB specifies “the troops” and makes their arrival a return. It says the ark will come “into our midst,” rendered “go with us” in BSB.
4.4: The Hebrew leaves the people sent unnamed and has no separate “back”; BSB supplies “men” and “back.” It also supplies “between” in describing the LORD’s place among the cherubim.
4.5: The Hebrew repeats the shouting root in the verb and “a great shout”; BSB expresses it as raising a shout.
4.6: The Hebrew repeats “the sound of the shout”; BSB varies the second occurrence as “loud shouting.”
4.7: The Hebrew’s coming verb is singular with Elohim; BSB uses plural “The gods have entered.” The time expression literally says “yesterday, the day before yesterday,” rendered “before” in BSB.
4.8: The Hebrew names Egypt collectively; BSB uses “the Egyptians.” It has singular “every plague,” rendered “all kinds of plagues” in BSB.
4.10: The Hebrew uses plural “his tents” distributively for each fleeing man; BSB uses singular “his tent.”
4.14: The Hebrew asks what the sound of this tumult is; BSB renders this as “Why this commotion?”
4.15: The Hebrew joins the fixed eyes and inability to see with “and”; BSB makes the latter an explicit “because” clause.
4.16: The Hebrew repeats “the battle line” as the place fled from; BSB substitutes “there.” It leaves the questioner unnamed, where BSB supplies Eli.
4.18: The Hebrew leaves Eli unnamed twice and describes his neck as being broken; BSB names Eli twice and says “he broke his neck.”
4.19: The Hebrew refers to “his daughter-in-law” without naming Eli; BSB supplies his name.
4.20: The Hebrew says she did not “set her heart” on the words; BSB renders this bodily expression as not paying heed.
4.21: The Hebrew refers simply to her father-in-law and husband after naming the ark’s capture; BSB supplies the explicit statement that they “had been killed.”

5.2: The Hebrew repeats the Philistines, the ark of God, and Dagon. BSB carries the first two forward implicitly and replaces the final Dagon with “his statue.” The temple is literally Dagon’s “house.”
5.4: The Hebrew explicitly names Dagon’s head and the two palms of his hands as “cut off”; BSB uses “his head and his hands broken off.” In the concluding clause the Hebrew retains Dagon’s name, where BSB says “the torso.”
5.5: The Hebrew explicitly calls the threshold “Dagon’s threshold”; BSB leaves that possessive implicit.
5.8: The Hebrew repeats “the ark of the God of Israel” in the instruction about Gath; BSB uses “It.”
5.9: The Hebrew refers to moving “it”; BSB supplies “the ark to Gath.” It describes the affected men as “from small to great,” rendered “both young and old” in BSB.
5.10: The Hebrew repeats the ark of God and Ekron at its arrival; BSB uses “it” and leaves the destination implicit. The Ekronites speak collectively with singular “me” and “my people,” rendered plural “us” and “our people” in BSB.
5.11: The Hebrew again uses singular “me and my people”; BSB has “us and our people.” The hand of God is described as “very heavy there,” where BSB has “heavy upon it.”

6.1: The Hebrew locates the ark in the “field of the Philistines”; BSB renders this as their “land.”
6.3: The Hebrew describes knowledge passively as something that “will be known to you”; BSB uses active “you will understand.” It says the hand does not “turn away” from them, rendered “has not been lifted” in BSB.
6.4: The Hebrew leaves the questioning speakers unnamed; BSB identifies them as the Philistines.
6.5: The Hebrew repeats “images” for the rats and calls them “your rats”; BSB leaves both implicit. It says God may make His hand light upon them, where BSB says He may “lift His hand.”
6.6: The Hebrew uses singular “your heart” and “their heart”; BSB uses plural “your hearts” and the implicit plural “theirs.”
6.7: The Hebrew says the yoke has not “gone up upon” the cows and commands bringing their young home from behind them. BSB renders these as having “never been yoked” and taking the calves away to pen them up.
6.9: The Hebrew leaves the responsible one as “he”; BSB explicitly supplies the LORD. The hand is described as having “touched us,” rendered “punished us” in BSB.
6.10: The Hebrew explicitly says the calves were confined “in the house”; BSB simply says “penned up.”
6.11: The Hebrew lists the chest, the gold rats, and the tumor images with repeated “and”; BSB explicitly presents the latter objects as contents of the chest.
6.13: The Hebrew says they lifted their eyes and rejoiced to see the ark; BSB uses “looked up” and “were overjoyed.”
6.14: The Hebrew says the cart stopped there and that a large stone was there, using two separate clauses. BSB combines them as stopping “near a large rock” and supplies “the people” as the ones chopping the cart.
6.17: The Hebrew lists the cities and repeats “one” for each gold tumor; BSB combines them under “one gold tumor for each city.”
6.19: The Hebrew lists “seventy men, fifty thousand men”; BSB states only “seventy men.” The Hebrew leaves the initial striking subject unnamed; BSB supplies God.
6.20: The Hebrew leaves the one to go up unnamed; BSB explicitly supplies “the ark.”
6.21: The Hebrew says to bring it up “to you”; BSB renders this as taking it up “with you.”

25.3: The Hebrew repeats “the woman” and “the man” in describing their characters; BSB uses “She” and “her husband.”
25.5: The Hebrew repeats David’s name before his instructions; BSB combines the instructions with his sending. It describes the greeting as asking about Nabal’s peace or welfare.
25.6: The Hebrew repeats “peace” for Nabal, his house, and all he owns; BSB combines these under one “peace.”
25.8: The Hebrew calls them “the young men,” where BSB supplies “my young men.” It uses the images of finding favor in the eyes and giving what the hand finds, rendered “find favor with you” and “whatever you can afford” in BSB.
25.10: The Hebrew explicitly calls the addressees “David’s servants”; BSB uses “them.”
25.12: The Hebrew describes returning and coming with two verbs; BSB combines these as “went back.”
25.13: The Hebrew repeats strapping on one’s sword for each man and then David separately. BSB combines David and his men under one action with plural “their swords.”
25.14: The Hebrew leaves the young man’s owner unnamed; BSB supplies Nabal. David’s messengers are said to come to “bless” the master, rendered “greet” in BSB.
25.15: The Hebrew describes their time together with a verb for walking about; BSB uses “lived among them.”
25.17: The Hebrew calls Nabal “a son of worthlessness”; BSB renders the image as “a scoundrel.”
25.20: The Hebrew leaves the woman unnamed and presents David and his men with “behold”; BSB supplies Abigail and says she saw them.
25.21: The Hebrew says David “had said,” without a separate reference to just finishing speaking; BSB says he “had just finished saying.”
25.22: The Hebrew’s oath names “David’s enemies,” where BSB names David. Its description of the threatened males literally says “one urinating against a wall,” rendered “one of Nabal’s men” in BSB.
25.24: The Hebrew asks to speak “in your ears”; BSB leaves the ears image implicit.
25.25: The Hebrew asks him not to “set his heart” on Nabal; BSB uses “pay no attention.” It repeats Nabal’s name in the name-and-folly wordplay, where BSB explicitly explains “His name means Fool.”
25.26: The Hebrew’s oath refers to “your soul” living; BSB says “you yourself” live. It describes self-help as the hand saving for oneself, rendered “avenging yourself with your own hand” in BSB.
25.27: The Hebrew calls the gift “this blessing” and describes the young men walking “at my lord’s feet.” BSB uses “this gift” and those who “follow you.”
25.28: The Hebrew promises a “faithful house”; BSB renders this as “a lasting dynasty.”
25.29: The Hebrew uses singular “soul of your enemies,” where BSB has plural “lives.” Its sling image explicitly names the sling’s palm or hollow; BSB instead supplies “like stones from a sling.”
25.31: The Hebrew describes a staggering and a stumbling of the heart; BSB renders these images as “remorse or guilt of conscience.” It describes self-vindication with the verb for saving oneself, where BSB uses “revenge.”
25.33: The Hebrew again describes David’s own hand saving for him; BSB renders this as “avenging myself by my own hand.”
25.34: The Hebrew repeats the description “one urinating against a wall”; BSB renders it as “no male belonging to Nabal.”
25.35: The Hebrew commands going “up” to her house and uses the image “I have lifted your face.” BSB leaves the upward direction implicit and renders the face image as “granted your request.”
25.36: The Hebrew says Nabal’s heart was good within him and that she told him no small or great matter. BSB uses “in high spirits” and compresses the small-and-great pair into “nothing.”
25.37: The Hebrew describes sobriety as the wine going out of Nabal and says his heart died within him. BSB has “Nabal was sober” and “his heart failed.”
25.38: The Hebrew separately says the LORD struck Nabal and that he died; BSB combines these as “struck Nabal dead.”
25.39: The Hebrew explicitly describes the reproach as coming “from Nabal’s hand”; BSB leaves the hand image implicit.
25.40: The Hebrew explicitly names “David’s servants”; BSB uses “his servants.”
25.42: The Hebrew describes the five attendants as going “at her foot”; BSB renders this as being “attended by five of her maidens.”
25.43: The Hebrew refers to both women without repeating their names; BSB supplies Abigail.

26.2: The Hebrew repeats “the wilderness of Ziph” as the search location; BSB replaces the second occurrence with “there.”
26.3: The Hebrew repeats Saul and the wilderness in describing his pursuit; BSB uses pronouns and “there.”
26.4: The Hebrew says David sent spies and then knew Saul had certainly come. BSB makes the verification the stated purpose of sending the spies.
26.5: The Hebrew repeats David as the one seeing the place; BSB uses “He.”
26.6: Abishai explicitly says he will go “down” with David; BSB leaves the downward direction implicit in his reply.
26.8: The Hebrew says he will not repeat the blow; BSB adds the explicit idea of necessity in “will not need to strike him twice.”
26.13: The Hebrew says the space between them was great; BSB specifies a “wide gulf.”
26.14: The Hebrew asks “Who are you who called to the king?”; BSB shortens this to “Who calls to the king?”
26.15: The Hebrew repeats “the king, your lord” as the threatened person; BSB uses “him.”
26.16: The Hebrew calls them “sons of death”; BSB renders the image as “deserve to die.”
26.19: The Hebrew wishes that the LORD may “smell an offering,” rendered “accept an offering” in BSB. The human instigators are called “sons of man,” rendered “men.”
26.21: The Hebrew says Saul’s soul was precious “in your eyes”; BSB uses “you considered my life precious.”
26.23: The Hebrew’s first reference to delivery says simply “into a hand”; BSB supplies “my hand.”
26.24: The Hebrew says his soul was great “in my eyes” and wishes his own soul to be great “in the eyes of the LORD.” BSB renders both as valuing a life.
26.25: The Hebrew emphatically repeats both the doing and prevailing roots; BSB adds “great things” for the first and “surely” for the second. Saul returns “to his place,” rendered “home” in BSB.

27.1: The Hebrew says David spoke “to his heart”; BSB uses “to himself.” The escape verb is emphatically repeated in Hebrew but appears once in BSB.
27.3: The Hebrew calls Abigail “Nabal’s wife”; BSB specifies “the widow of Nabal.”
27.4: The Hebrew says passively that Saul was told; BSB uses active “Saul learned.”
27.5: The Hebrew requests that unnamed people “give me a place”; BSB makes this passive “let me be assigned a place.”
27.6: The Hebrew repeats Ziklag’s name as belonging to Judah’s kings; BSB uses “it.”
27.7: The Hebrew’s time expression literally uses “days and four months”; BSB renders the period as “a year and four months.”
27.8: The Hebrew uses collective singular names for the Geshurite, Girzite, and Amalekite; BSB uses plural ethnic names.
27.9: The Hebrew separately says David returned and came to Achish; BSB combines these as “return to Achish.”
27.10: The Hebrew explicitly names Achish as questioner and joins the three Negev regions with “and”; BSB uses a relative clause for Achish and separates the answers with “or.”
27.11: The Hebrew describes the territory as “the field of the Philistines”; BSB uses “Philistine territory.”
27.12: The Hebrew introduces Achish’s words with “saying”; BSB uses “thinking.”

28.2: The Hebrew calls the promised position “keeper of my head”; BSB renders the head image as “my bodyguard.”
28.4: The Hebrew says “they camped” at Gilboa after Saul gathered Israel; BSB makes Saul the continuing subject of “camped.”
28.5: The Hebrew says Saul’s heart trembled greatly; BSB makes Saul himself the subject of trembling.
28.6: The Hebrew explicitly names Saul as the inquirer; BSB uses “He.”
28.7: The Hebrew describes the woman as a possessor of a spirit; BSB uses the role name “a medium.”
28.8: The Hebrew leaves the speaker at the woman’s house unnamed and includes a request particle; BSB names Saul and leaves the request particle implicit.
28.9: The Hebrew uses collective singular for the spiritist and describes setting a trap for her soul. BSB uses plural “spiritists” and leaves the soul image implicit.
28.12: The Hebrew repeats “the woman” before her speech; BSB combines her seeing, crying out, and speaking under one subject.
28.13: The Hebrew has a plural ascending participle with Elohim; BSB uses singular “a god coming up.”
28.14: The Hebrew leaves the questioner unnamed; BSB supplies Saul.
28.15: The Hebrew explicitly says God does not answer “by the hand of the prophets”; BSB leaves the hand image implicit.
28.17: The Hebrew names the LORD in the first clause and says He spoke “by my hand”; BSB uses “He” and “through me.”
28.18: The Hebrew says Saul did not listen “to the voice of the LORD”; BSB renders this as not obeying the LORD.
28.20: The Hebrew describes Saul falling to the ground in the fullness of his height and says he had eaten no bread. BSB uses “fell flat” and had not eaten “anything.”
28.21: The Hebrew says she placed her soul in her singular palm; BSB uses “life in my hands.” It explicitly says she heard his words, where BSB says she “did as you told me.”
28.22: The Hebrew asks Saul to hear “the voice of your maidservant”; BSB leaves the voice image implicit.
28.23: The Hebrew leaves Saul unnamed as the one refusing; BSB supplies his name.

29.2: The Hebrew says the Philistine rulers passed in hundreds and thousands; BSB explicitly makes them marching out “their units.”
29.3: The Hebrew explicitly names the Philistine commanders as the recipients of Achish’s reply and joins days and years with “or.” BSB leaves the addressees implicit and uses “days, even years.”
29.4: The Hebrew twice names “the commanders of the Philistines” and says the man may win favor by “the heads of those men.” BSB names the commanders once and renders the heads as those “of our men.”
29.6: The Hebrew says his going out and coming in are good “in my eyes”; BSB attaches “in my sight” to his uprightness and says the marching “seems right.”
29.7: The Hebrew says not to do evil “in the eyes of the Philistine rulers”; BSB renders this as doing nothing to displease them.
29.8: The Hebrew describes David’s service as being “before you”; BSB renders this as having come to Achish.
29.9: The Hebrew explicitly says the commanders prohibited going “up” with them into battle; BSB leaves the upward direction implicit.
29.10: The Hebrew repeats rising early in the morning, shifting from singular to plural address; BSB combines this into one instruction to rise early.

30.1: The Hebrew repeats Ziklag three times and uses the collective singular Amalekite; BSB names Ziklag twice and uses plural “Amalekites.”
30.2: The Hebrew names “the women who were in it, from small to great”; BSB adds “and all who were there” and renders the size pair as “both young and old.”
30.4: The Hebrew calls the accompanying group “the people” and uses singular “their voice”; BSB has “the troops” and plural “their voices.”
30.5: The Hebrew calls Abigail “Nabal’s wife”; BSB specifies “the widow of Nabal.”
30.6: The Hebrew says the people’s soul was “bitter”; BSB says each man’s soul “grieved.”
30.7: The Hebrew repeats both the ephod and David in the final bringing; BSB replaces both with pronouns. It also has a request particle in David’s instruction.
30.8: The Hebrew names the raiding band collectively in the singular; BSB uses plural “raiders.” Both overtaking and rescuing have emphatic root repetition; BSB supplies “the captives” as the object of rescue.
30.10: The Hebrew states David’s pursuit before the two hundred men remaining; BSB puts their exhaustion first. The Hebrew repeats the name Besor, where BSB uses “the brook.”
30.11: The Hebrew leaves the finders unnamed and says they gave him bread and he ate, then gave him water. BSB supplies “his men,” reverses the order of food and water, and renders bread as “food.”
30.12: The Hebrew says his spirit returned to him; BSB renders this as “was revived.” It calls the food he lacked “bread.”
30.13: The Hebrew explicitly calls him an Egyptian young man; BSB leaves his youth implicit.
30.15: The Hebrew twice says to lead him “down” to the raiding band; BSB leaves both downward directions implicit.
30.16: The Hebrew leaves both the man led and the raiders unnamed; BSB supplies David and “the Amalekites.”
30.18: The Hebrew separately says David rescued everything and rescued his two wives, repeating his name and the rescue verb. BSB combines the wives into the first recovery statement.
30.19: The Hebrew has plural “sons and daughters” and leaves the plunder-takers unnamed; BSB uses singular “son or daughter” and supplies “the Amalekites.”
30.20: The Hebrew names David as the one taking the livestock and leaves its drivers unnamed; BSB uses “he” for David and supplies “his men” as drivers.
30.21: The Hebrew repeats David’s name four times and explicitly says the exhausted men had been made to stay at Besor. BSB names him twice and leaves the causation of staying implicit.
30.22: The Hebrew quotes singular “they did not go with me”; BSB uses plural “with us.”
30.23: The Hebrew uses singular “our hand”; BSB uses plural “our hands.”
30.24: The Hebrew describes one going “down” to battle and one sitting with the equipment; BSB leaves the downward direction implicit and says “stayed with the supplies.”
30.25: The Hebrew leaves the lawgiver unnamed; BSB supplies David.
30.26: The Hebrew calls the gift “a blessing” and uses singular “his friend” collectively; BSB has “a gift” and plural “his friends.”
30.27: The Hebrew continues the recipient list without repeating a sending verb or gift noun; BSB supplies “He sent gifts.”
30.29: The Hebrew repeats “cities” for the Kenite and uses collective singular ethnic names; BSB combines the two groups under one “cities” and uses plural ethnic names.

31.1: The Hebrew repeats the Philistines as those fled from and has no separate word for “many” among the slain. BSB uses “them” and supplies “many.”
31.2: The Hebrew repeats the Philistines as those striking Saul’s sons; BSB uses “they.”
31.3: The Hebrew says the archers found him, repeating the archers in describing his suffering; BSB uses “overtook him” and leaves the repeated archers implicit.
31.4: The Hebrew says Saul took “the sword”; BSB specifies “his own sword.”
31.7: The Hebrew says “the men of Israel” fled and that the Philistines dwelt in the abandoned cities. BSB uses “the army of Israel” and “occupied their cities.”
31.9: The Hebrew leaves Saul unnamed and the people sent unnamed; BSB supplies Saul and “messengers.” It has singular “the house of their idols,” rendered plural “the temples of their idols.”
31.10: The Hebrew says they fastened his body to the wall; BSB uses “hung his body.”
